<br>

## Packages

<br>

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

<br>

## Datasets

<br>

The chosen dataset to be studied was **"US Groceries and Gas Prices (2015-2026)."**

We decided that this dataset is relevant to current social and economic issues faced by many U.S. citizens, specifically the increasing cost of groceries and energy.

There are three versions of the same dataset. Three analyses will be performed, and one main dataset will be used to investigate the research question:

**How have grocery and fuel prices changed in the United States between 2015 and 2026, and which categories experienced the highest prices over time?**

<br>

```{r}
avg_item_summary <- read.csv(file.choose(), header = TRUE)
avg_price_monthly <- read.csv(file.choose(), header = TRUE)
avg_price_wide <- read.csv(file.choose(), header = TRUE)
```

<br>

## Average Price Monthly Analysis

<br>

```{r}
avg_price_monthly %>%
  glimpse()

summary(avg_price_monthly)
```

<br>

Some of the columns are not necessary for this project and will be removed, such as *series_id*. Additionally, *year*, *month*, and *category* will be converted to factors so they can be treated as categorical variables during analysis.

<br>

```{r}
avg_price_mo <- avg_price_monthly %>%
  select(-series_id) %>%
  mutate(
    category = factor(
      category,
      levels = c(
        "Meat, broad category",
        "Pork and deli",
        "Beef",
        "Drinks",
        "Dairy and fats",
        "Energy",
        "Fruit",
        "Vegetables",
        "Bakery and grains",
        "Poultry",
        "Eggs",
        "Pantry and snacks"
      )
    ),
    year = factor(year),
    month = factor(month),
    date = as.Date(date)
  )
```

<br>

# Summary

<br>

There are 8,869 observations and 8 variables in the dataset.

The *date*, *year*, and *month* variables describe when an observation was recorded. The data covers the period from 2015 through 2026.

The *item* variable provides detailed descriptions of products, while *category* groups these products into broader classifications.

The *unit* variable indicates the measurement unit associated with the item.

The *price* variable contains the average observed price and serves as the primary variable of interest for this analysis.

<br>

```{r}
dim(avg_price_mo)

summary(avg_price_mo)
```

<br>

## Visualizing Categories

<br>

To understand which product categories tend to have the highest prices, the average price for each category is calculated and visualized below.

<br>

```{r}
avg_price_mo %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = reorder(category, mean_price),
    y = mean_price
  )) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Price by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Average Price"
  )
```

<br>

The graph suggests that the **Beef** category tends to have some of the highest average prices among all food categories. To explore this category further, only Beef products will be examined.

<br>

```{r}
only_beef <- avg_price_mo %>%
  filter(category == "Beef") %>%
  mutate(item = factor(item))
```

<br>

## Beef Category Exploration

<br>

The following visualization displays the individual Beef products across time, allowing trends and possible outliers to be observed.

<br>

```{r}
only_beef %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = price)) +
  geom_line(color = "black") +
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~item, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Beef Prices Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Price"
  )
```

<br>

## Distribution of Prices by Category

<br>

A boxplot can be used to compare the distribution of prices across categories and identify variation and potential outliers.

<br>

```{r}
ggplot(
  avg_price_mo,
  aes(
    x = category,
    y = price,
    fill = category
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Price Distribution by Category",
    x = "Category",
    y = "Price"
  )
```

<br>

The boxplot demonstrates that price variability differs substantially across categories. Some categories exhibit wider distributions and more extreme values than others.

<br>

## Price Trends Over Time

<br>

To determine whether prices have generally increased over time, average prices are plotted across the study period for all categories.

<br>

```{r}
avg_price_mo %>%
  group_by(date, category) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_price = mean(price, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = date,
      y = avg_price,
      color = category
    )
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Price Trends by Category",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Average Price",
    color = "Category"
  )
```

<br>

The trend plot indicates that prices generally increased across many grocery and energy categories between 2015 and 2026. While some categories remained relatively stable, others experienced substantial increases during the observed period.

<br>

# Conclusion

<br>

This exploratory analysis examined grocery and fuel prices in the United States from 2015 through 2026.

The results suggest that price levels vary considerably among product categories, with Beef consistently appearing among the highest-priced categories. The boxplot analysis also revealed substantial variation within categories, while the time-series analysis indicated that many categories experienced increasing prices over time.

Future analyses could investigate specific products that experienced the largest price increases and determine whether certain categories were more affected by inflationary pressures than others.
